people.name: Getatchew Haile
people.field: Scholarship: Ethiopian languages, manuscripts and church history
body: For four decades a scholar at the Hill Museum & Manuscript Library at Saint John's University in Collegeville, Minnesota, read and described Ethiopian manuscripts that had been microfilmed in Ethiopia's churches and monasteries. Many were written in Ge'ez, the ancient language of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose script Amharic also uses. His catalogs changed the field, in the library's words, and scholars around the world still rely on them.

Getatchew was born in rural Shenkora, Ethiopia, in 1931. His family's obituary describes a modest childhood marked by upheaval and homelessness during the Italian occupation. He studied at Holy Trinity Spiritual School in Addis Ababa, earned a B.A. from the American University in Cairo and a B.D. from the Coptic Theological College in Cairo, both in 1957, and took a Ph.D. at the University of Tübingen in Germany in 1962. Back home he served briefly in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and then taught for ten years at Haile Selassie I University, now Addis Ababa University. He married Misrak Amare in 1964.

After the Derg came to power, he served in the short-lived civilian parliament, representing Shoa, and spoke out for democracy and the separation of church and state. In October 1975 soldiers tried to arrest him for those views and shot him. He survived and was left a paraplegic. After medical care in England he reached Saint John's in 1976. He became Regents Professor of Medieval Studies and curator of the library's Ethiopia Study Center. By the library's account, he had published descriptions of several thousand manuscripts by 1993.

He received a MacArthur Fellowship in 1988 and the British Academy's Edward Ullendorff Medal in 2013, and was elected a corresponding member of the British Academy in 1987. The family obituary calls him the first Ethiopian and first African to receive the MacArthur and to join the British Academy. He also published the magazine Ethiopian Register and served his church in many roles. He moved to New York City in 2016 to be nearer family, kept working, and died there on June 10, 2021. His funeral was held at Saint John's Abbey Church. His family says his one regret was never being able to return to Ethiopia.
keyFacts: 1931: Born in Shenkora, Ethiopia.
October 1975: Shot during an attempted arrest by Derg soldiers; left a paraplegic.
1976: Arrives at the Hill Museum & Manuscript Library in Collegeville, Minnesota.
1987: Corresponding member of the British Academy. 1988: MacArthur Fellowship. 2013: Edward Ullendorff Medal.
June 10, 2021: Dies in New York City; funeral June 18 at Saint John's Abbey Church.

people.name: Rebecca Haile
body: Rebecca Haile was born in Ethiopia and lived there until she was eleven. Her father, the scholar Getatchew Haile, was shot when soldiers came to arrest him. In 1976 the family reached central Minnesota as refugees, and she has written that scholarships and good schools were what made the new start work. She went on to Williams College and Harvard Law School.

About 25 years after the family fled, she became the first of them to go back. She wrote about that trip in Held at a Distance (Academy Chicago Publishers, 2007), a memoir that mixes travel, history and family story. Her education initiative's page describes her as fluent in English and Amharic.

She kept returning. In 2016 she and her husband, Jean Manas, started Ethiopia Education Initiatives, a U.S.-based nonprofit. Its first project, Haile-Manas Academy, is a boarding school in Debre Birhan that admits students without regard to their ability to pay. It welcomed its first 35 students in January 2021 and, by her account, graduated its first class in May 2024. Tadias Magazine reported in 2021 that she had been elected board chair of EMILY's List and lived in New York City.
keyFacts: 1965: Born in Ethiopia.
1976: Reaches Minnesota with her family, as a refugee, at age eleven.
2007: Publishes Held at a Distance.
2016: Co-founds Ethiopia Education Initiatives.
May 2024: Haile-Manas Academy graduates its first class.

people.name: Henok A. Degfu
body: Henok Degfu was born in Addis Ababa in 1983 and became a journalist young. By Sahan Journal's account he was jailed five times in Ethiopia. In February 2005, after the government filed 12 defamation cases against him, he left the country. He paid smugglers for a desert crossing to Libya, spent three months in a Benghazi jail, was deported to the Sudan border, and later paid for a place on an inflatable boat to Turkey.

In 2007 he petitioned the UN refugee agency, and the United States eventually granted him asylum. In 2008, months after arriving in Minnesota, he started ZeHabesha, first a 24-page monthly newspaper in English and Amharic. "Habesha" is a word some Ethiopians and Eritreans use for themselves. By mid-2020 ZeHabesha had a studio off Snelling Avenue in St. Paul, more than 600,000 YouTube subscribers and about 1.3 million Facebook followers. Its five full-time reporters work in Ethiopia, and he does not name them, citing their safety.

In May 2020 Ethiopian Airlines, which the Ethiopian government owns, sued him and ZeHabesha for $25 million for defamation in U.S. District Court in Minnesota. The suit concerns three YouTube interviews that made allegations about the airline and its chief executive, and the airline denies them. His lawyer said he would respond in a counterfiling. No public report of how the case ended was found.
keyFacts: 1983: Born in Addis Ababa.
February 2005: Leaves Ethiopia after 12 defamation cases are filed against him.
2008: Founds ZeHabesha in Minnesota.
May 2020: Named in a $25 million defamation suit by Ethiopian Airlines; outcome not publicly reported in the sources found.

people.name: Hailu Mergia
body: In the 1970s Hailu Mergia played organ and accordion with the Walias Band in the Addis Ababa nightclub scene, in the sound now called Ethio-jazz. In 1981 the band toured the United States, and he stayed. In 1984 he formed the Zula Band with Moges Habte and Tamiru Ayele, which lasted until 1991. He then worked in the African nightclub business, and in 1998 began driving a cab in the Washington, D.C., area.

In 2013 Brian Shimkovitz, whose label Awesome Tapes from Africa reissues African cassette music, reissued his earlier work, and his career revived. His album Lala Belu came out in March 2018 to strong reviews. That October, at 71, he played his first Twin Cities show, at the Cedar Cultural Center in Minneapolis, with the Yohannes Tona Band. He told the Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder he had just quit the cab to focus on music.
keyFacts: 1981: Stays in the United States after a Walias Band tour.
1984–1991: The Zula Band.
1998: Begins driving a cab.
2013: Awesome Tapes from Africa reissue revives his career.
October 26, 2018: Plays the Cedar Cultural Center in Minneapolis.

people.name: Aster Aweke
body: Aster Aweke was born around 1960 in or near Gondar and raised in Addis Ababa, where her father was a senior civil servant in the imperial government. She had decided on music by 13 and was singing in clubs and hotels in her late teens. In 1977 she joined the Shebele Band, and music entrepreneur Ali Tango released her first cassettes.

In 1981 she left for the United States, first to the San Francisco Bay Area, and in 1983 moved to Washington, D.C., to sing regularly at a restaurant. Her album Aster came out in 1989 on Triple Earth and Columbia. Later albums include Hagere (1999), Fikir (2006) and Checheho (2010). In 1997 she returned to Ethiopia for the first time since 1981, for a month-long tour that drew large crowds.
keyFacts: About 1960: Born in or near Gondar; raised in Addis Ababa.
1977: Joins the Shebele Band.
1981: Moves to the United States.
1989: Aster released on Triple Earth and Columbia.
1997: First return to Ethiopia since 1981.

people.name: Ephraim Isaac
body: In the late 1960s, when Harvard University was building its African and Afro-American Studies department, its first faculty appointment was Ephraim Isaac, a scholar born in Ethiopia. Sources give 1968 or 1969 for the start. He taught there until 1977, and Harvard established a prize in African Studies in his name in 1998.

He was born around 1936 in Nejo, in Wollega. His father, a teacher in the Yemenite Jewish tradition, taught him the Hebrew Bible. He earned a bachelor of divinity at Harvard Divinity School in 1963 and became the first Ethiopian-born person to take a Harvard Ph.D. He is also known in Ethiopia as the founder of a national literacy campaign that, by his biographers' accounts, helped millions learn to read.

He chaired an ad hoc peace committee that My Jewish Learning credits with helping end the Ethiopia–Eritrea war, and he received a 2002 Peacemaker Award from the Tanenbaum Center for Interreligious Understanding. Fellowship in Prayer's board page lists him as director of the Institute of Semitic Studies in Princeton and chair of the Ethiopian Peace and Development Center.
keyFacts: About 1936: Born in Nejo, Wollega.
1963: Bachelor of divinity, Harvard Divinity School; later a Harvard Ph.D.
Late 1960s to 1977: Teaches at Harvard.
1998: Harvard establishes the Ephraim Isaac Prize in African Studies.
2002: Tanenbaum Peacemaker Award.

people.name: Wosene Worke Kosrof
body: Wosene Worke Kosrof paints with letters. His signature style, which he calls WordPlay, reshapes the fidel, the script used to write Amharic, into images and patterns, so that writing itself becomes the picture.

By his AGNI author profile, he was born in 1950 in the Arat Kilo area of Addis Ababa. He earned a BFA at the School of Fine Arts in Addis Ababa in 1972 and an MFA at Howard University in Washington, D.C., in 1980. He lives and has his studio in Berkeley, California. The same profile calls him the first Ethiopian-born artist to use Amharic script forms in contemporary fine art, and says his work is in museum and private collections.
keyFacts: 1950: Born in Addis Ababa, by his AGNI profile.
1972: BFA, School of Fine Arts, Addis Ababa.
1980: MFA, Howard University.
Studio in Berkeley, California.

people.name: Haile Gerima
body: Haile Gerima was born in Gondar on March 4, 1946. He came to the United States to study acting and directing at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and later completed the master's program in film at UCLA. He has taught for more than 25 years in Howard University's Department of Radio, Television, and Film.

His films include Harvest: 3,000 Years (1976), shot in Ethiopia with non-professional actors, which won a top prize at the Locarno Film Festival; Bush Mama (1979); Ashes and Embers (1982); and Sankofa (1993), about slavery and memory. In 1996 he founded Sankofa Video and Bookstore in Washington, D.C. Teza (2008), an Amharic-language film about an Ethiopian doctor who returns from Germany to a country in political turmoil, won the Special Jury Prize and the Golden Osella for best screenplay at the Venice Film Festival.
keyFacts: March 4, 1946: Born in Gondar.
1976: Harvest: 3,000 Years.
1993: Sankofa.
1996: Founds Sankofa Video and Bookstore, Washington, D.C.
2008: Teza wins two awards at Venice.

people.name: Liya Kebede
body: Liya Kebede was born in Addis Ababa in 1978. In 2000 designer Tom Ford signed her to an exclusive deal with Gucci, and she later became Estée Lauder's first Black spokesmodel. She has appeared on many magazine covers and acted in films.

In 2005 the World Health Organization named her a goodwill ambassador for maternal, newborn and child health. Her foundation works to raise awareness of maternal deaths and supports programs that address them; in 2011 it opened a maternity center in Hawassa, Ethiopia. In 2007 she launched lemlem, a clothing line made with Ethiopian hand-weavers. Lemlem means "to bloom" or "flourish" in Amharic.

people.name: Meklit Hadero
body: By her official biography, Meklit Hadero was born in Ethiopia and moved with her family to Iowa at age two. She spent much of her adolescence in Brooklyn, studied political science at Yale, lived in Seattle, and settled in San Francisco, where she built a career as a singer-songwriter who works in Amharic and English.

Her earlier band, Nefasha Ayer, took its name from an Amharic phrase meaning "the wind that travels." As a TED Senior Fellow she launched the Arba Minch Collective, a group of Ethiopian artists abroad who work with artists in Ethiopia. Her albums include On a Day Like This... (2010), We Are Alive (2014) and When the People Move, the Music Moves Too (2017).
keyFacts: Born in Ethiopia; moved to Iowa at age two.
B.A., Yale University; based in San Francisco.
TED Senior Fellow; launched the Arba Minch Collective.

people.name: Mulugeta Seraw
body: Mulugeta Seraw was born on October 21, 1960, and moved to Portland, Oregon, from Addis Ababa in 1981. He studied business at Portland Community College and drove a bus for Avis at the airport. In November 1988, outside his apartment, three young white supremacists beat him with a baseball bat. He died in the hospital hours later, on November 13, at 28. The sources reviewed describe him as Ethiopian and do not state his first language.

His attackers belonged to the skinhead gang East Side White Pride, which had ties to White Aryan Resistance, a national hate group run from California by Tom Metzger. All three took plea bargains. Kenneth Mieske received a life sentence, Kyle Brewster 10 years and Steven Strasser six.

On November 22, 1989, the Southern Poverty Law Center filed Berhanu v. Metzger on behalf of his estate, represented by Engedaw Berhanu. The suit argued that Metzger, his son John and their group had sent a recruiter to organize the Portland gang. On October 25, 1990, a Multnomah County jury awarded his family $12.5 million. In 1994 the U.S. Supreme Court declined to review the appeal, and proceeds from the sale of the group's assets went to the family. His son, Henock, was the principal beneficiary.
keyFacts: October 21, 1960: Born in Ethiopia.
1981: Moves to Portland from Addis Ababa.
November 13, 1988: Dies after a racist attack in Portland.
October 25, 1990: Jury awards his family $12.5 million.
1994: U.S. Supreme Court declines to review the appeal.

people.name: Mehret Mandefro
body: In 2014 Difret, an Ethiopian film about a women's rights case that led to a ban on kidnapping child brides, won audience awards at both Sundance and Berlin. One of its producers was a physician, Mehret Mandefro.

She was born in Ethiopia. She earned a bachelor's degree and a medical degree at Harvard, an MSc from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine as a Fulbright Scholar, and a Ph.D. in cultural anthropology at Temple University. She has worked with communities affected by HIV in Botswana, South Africa, Ethiopia and New York, and was a White House Fellow and health policy advisor in the Office of the Secretary of Veterans Affairs under President Obama. She has also taught health policy at George Washington University.

She co-founded and, by the Carnegie Corporation's account, leads Truth Aid, which makes films about the social conditions that shape health. Her credits include All of Us, about her HIV research, and Little White Lie for PBS's Independent Lens. She is also an executive producer at Kana Television. Carnegie named her one of its Great Immigrants in 2016. The sources reviewed do not say whether she uses Amharic.

Harvard B.A. and M.D.; MSc, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine; Ph.D., Temple University.

people.name: Alemtsehay Wedajo
body: Alemtsehay Wedajo began performing professionally at 13. She studied theater in Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Germany and the Soviet Union, and was named the first woman director of the Ethiopian National Theater. She co-founded the Ethiopian Actors Association and chaired it for fourteen years, and she created YeLijoch Amba, described as Ethiopia's first children's theater group, which trained children, many of them orphans, in music, drama and the arts.

She moved to the United States in 1991. In the Washington, D.C., area she founded and personally funded what is now the Tayitu Cultural and Educational Center, whose first event, a book release and reading, came in August 2000. By Tayitu's account she has written lyrics for more than forty popular Ethiopian songs, sung by artists including Aster Aweke, and she tours with its troupe in North America and Europe. She published poetry collections in 1996 and 2010.
keyFacts: Begins performing at 13; first woman director of the Ethiopian National Theater.
Founds YeLijoch Amba, a children's theater group in Ethiopia.

August 2000: First event of what becomes the Tayitu center.

people.name: Daniel W. Yohannes
body: Daniel Yohannes was born in Addis Ababa on September 22, 1952. He came to the United States at 17 as an exchange student, attended high school in Los Angeles, and worked as a stock-room clerk and a bank teller. He earned a bachelor's degree in economics at Claremont McKenna College in 1976 and an MBA at Pepperdine University in 1980. The sources reviewed do not say whether he uses Amharic.

He joined Security Pacific National Bank as a management trainee in 1977 and rose to executive vice president. In 1992 he moved to Denver as president and CEO of Colorado National Bank, then led U.S. Bank's Colorado operations, and in 2006 he co-founded New Resource Bank.

In 2009 President Obama chose him to lead the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a U.S. foreign aid agency, and he served more than four years. The Senate confirmed him as U.S. Ambassador to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development on April 9, 2014, and National Jewish Health lists that service as running to 2017. It also lists him as a member of its board.
keyFacts: September 22, 1952: Born in Addis Ababa.
1992–1998: President and CEO of Colorado National Bank.
2009–2014: CEO, Millennium Challenge Corporation.
2014–2017: U.S. Ambassador to the OECD.

people.name: Samra Brouk
body: Samra Brouk was born and raised in Rochester, New York, the daughter of Ethiopian immigrants. By Tadias Magazine's account, her father fled Ethiopia during the civil war and earned degrees in math and engineering in Western New York, and her mother was a public school teacher. The sources reviewed do not say whether her family speaks Amharic.

She earned a psychology degree at Williams College, served in the Peace Corps as a health educator in rural Guatemala, and spent about a decade in nonprofit work. In November 2020 she won New York's 55th Senate District, Rochester and its eastern suburbs, and began her term in January 2021 as the first Black woman to represent it. She won re-election in 2022.
As of October 2026 the New York State Senate lists her as senator for District 55 and chair of its Mental Health Committee. Her seat is on the ballot in the general election of November 3, 2026.

people.name: Yetnebersh Nigussie
body: Yetnebersh Nigussie was born on January 24, 1982, in the Amhara region of Ethiopia. She became blind at five after meningitis. She escaped an early marriage and was sent to the Shashemane Catholic school for blind children. She went on to earn a law degree and a master's degree in social work at Addis Ababa University, and chaired the Blind Women's Wing of the Ethiopian National Association of the Blind for four years.

In 2005 she co-founded the Ethiopian Centre for Disability and Development, and she was its executive director from 2011 to 2015. In 2016 she joined Light for the World as a senior inclusion advisor. She received the 2017 Right Livelihood Award for her work on the rights and inclusion of people with disabilities. Her message, on the award's page: "Focus on the person, not the disability."

2005: Co-founds the Ethiopian Centre for Disability and Development.

people.name: Zemi Yenus
body: Zemi Yenus was the mother of Jojo, an autistic son. After his diagnosis she used her savings to open the Joy Center in 2002, in a small rented house in Addis Ababa with four students. By The Transmitter's account it was Ethiopia's first school for autistic children, and by 2017 it had more than 80 students and a waiting list more than twice that size.

She developed ABUGIDA Fonetics, a language and speech curriculum, and taught the Addis Ababa taxi association about autism. Some taxis began displaying signs as autism-friendly and gave free rides to autistic children and their parents. She hosted the radio program Yagebagnal, helped adapt the World Health Organization's Caregiver Skills Training for Ethiopia, and advised that home visitors should not accept refreshments, so that families would not strain their budgets. She died of COVID-19 on May 11, 2021, at 60.
keyFacts: 2002: Founds the Joy Center in Addis Ababa.
Developed the ABUGIDA Fonetics curriculum.
Helped adapt the WHO's Caregiver Skills Training for Ethiopia.

institutions.name: Re'ese Adbarat Tserha Aryam Kidist Selassie Cathedral
institutions.type: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo cathedral with community programs
body: By the cathedral's own history, on April 13, 2014, more than 500 Ethiopian Orthodox parishioners in Minneapolis chose to join the structure of the Holy Synod in Ethiopia. They held their first full Divine Liturgy outside their old building on Easter Sunday, April 20, and Archbishop Abune Zecharias blessed the name Tserha Aryam Kidist Selassie (Holy Trinity) that May.

On December 31, 2014, they bought a building on Minnehaha Avenue and rebuilt its interior. Archbishops Abune Zecharias and Abune Markos consecrated it on August 1–2, 2015. That December, Patriarch Abba Matthias I visited and raised it to cathedral status. The church houses Medhanealem's Holy Ark.

Its website lists Sunday school and choir, Saturday language education, Friday faith education, youth development, parent and family programs, an English service, faith community nursing, mentoring and social services, a scholarship and an annual 5K run. It describes itself as under the Minnesota and Surrounding Archdiocese. Its office number is 612-913-7000.
keyFacts: April 13, 2014: More than 500 parishioners align with the Holy Synod in Ethiopia.
December 31, 2014: Building purchased.
August 1–2, 2015: Consecrated.
December 19–20, 2015: Raised to cathedral status during the Patriarch's visit.
institutions.connectToWork: If you plan outreach through a parish, how would you learn what it already offers and which other congregations you would miss by going only there?

institutions.name: Ethiopian Community Development Council
institutions.type: Refugee resettlement and community development nonprofit
institutions.location: Arlington, Virginia, with sites across the U.S.
body: In 1983 Tsehaye Teferra, an Ethiopian immigrant who earned his MS and Ph.D. at Georgetown University, founded the council as a community-based nonprofit in Arlington. By its own account, in 1991 it became the first community-based organization authorized by the U.S. Department of State to resettle refugees.

It opened branch offices in Denver (2001) and Las Vegas (2002), and in Wausau, Wisconsin, and Brattleboro, Vermont, in 2021. Its home page says it is one of nine national refugee resettlement agencies funded by the Department of State, with 7 branch offices and 17 affiliate sites. Its pages do not list a Minnesota site. Its programs include resettlement, financial literacy and humanitarian assistance.
keyFacts: 1983: Founded in Arlington, Virginia.
1991: First community-based organization authorized to resettle refugees, by its own account.
2026 home page: 7 branch offices and 17 affiliate sites; no Minnesota site listed.
institutions.connectToWork: When you need a resettlement partner, do you ask who built that agency and who it answers to, and how would that change what you ask of it?

institutions.name: Tayitu Cultural and Educational Center
institutions.type: Arts, theater and youth education center
institutions.location: Washington, D.C., and Silver Spring, Maryland
body: After moving to the United States in 1991, the playwright and lyricist Alemtsehay Wedajo founded and personally funded a cultural center in the Washington area. Tadias Magazine dates its first event, as Tayitu Entertainment, to August 2000.

The center produces theater aimed at youth, women and children's welfare, offers a forum for literary works, and provides academic support and mentoring for young people. It describes itself as a home for Ethiopian artists in the diaspora, and its troupe tours for Ethiopian audiences in North America and Europe.
keyFacts: August 2000: First event, as Tayitu Entertainment.
Addresses: 1101 30th Street NW, Washington, D.C., and 8209 Fenton Street, Silver Spring, Maryland.
Programs: theater and literary productions; youth academic support and mentoring.
institutions.connectToWork: Is there a Minnesota group doing this kind of work with children and parents, and if your program does not know, who would you ask?

institutions.name: Ethiopian Eritrean Special Needs Community
institutions.location: Olney, Maryland; works in Maryland, Virginia and Washington, D.C.
body: Its tagline is "Building Bridges to Empower Autistic Individuals and Their Families." Its Candid profile says it works on language barriers, stigma, limited awareness and the difficulty of navigating education, health care and disability systems, including by translating key resources into Amharic and Tigrinya.

It lists caregiver skills training, outreach through faith-based and other organizations, developmental screening, and a cultural arts program, which it says engaged 10 adults with special needs in 2025. It says it has reached more than 1,500 caregivers, parents, family members and community participants since 2019. Its president, Azeb Adere, is listed on the profile; Azeb Ataro Adere is lead author of the 2023 survey of Ethiopian and Eritrean parents of autistic children in the United States. It is not based in Minnesota.
keyFacts: Serves Maryland, Virginia and Washington, D.C.
Translates key resources into Amharic and Tigrinya.
Programs: caregiver skills training, outreach, developmental screening, cultural arts.
institutions.connectToWork: Who in Minnesota is doing this work in Amharic now, and if you cannot name anyone, what would it take for your office to find out or to fund it?

sources.label: Candid (GuideStar), Ethiopian Eritrean Special Needs Community profile
University of Maryland, summary of Adere, Dababnah and Habayeb (2023), Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions and describes no person or family. No study of how Amharic speakers in Minnesota understand disability was found. What follows comes from one U.S. survey about autism, studies in Ethiopia that may not apply to families here, and one piece of journalism. People who speak Amharic include Ethiopian Orthodox, Protestant, Muslim and Catholic people from different regions, generations and educational backgrounds. The sources say little about how views differ across those lines.
questions: What do you call this at home, and what words would you like me to use?
Do you want an interpreter, and if so, in which language, and do you have a preference about their gender or whether they come from outside your local community?
Would you like to tell me what you or your family think caused this, or would you rather not?
Who gave you a label, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open for you, and what do you want it to avoid?
Who do you want involved in this decision, and what do you want to decide for yourself?
Is prayer, holy water or church support part of your care, and how should our services fit around it, including fasting periods and pilgrimages?
What have you heard about this from relatives or your church, and what would you like to know more about?
What would it cost you to take part in this, in time off work, transportation or waiting?
Would you like to meet other parents or people in your own language, or would you rather not?
Do you want written materials, and in which language and script, or would you rather hear this spoken?
What do you want to know about who will see your information, and whether it reaches immigration authorities?

context.heading: A U.S. survey of parents of autistic children
body: Adere, Dababnah and Habayeb (2023) ran an online survey of 51 Ethiopian and Eritrean parents raising autistic children in the United States. The University of Maryland's summary says no earlier research existed on these families. Parents reported limited knowledge of autism in their communities before diagnosis, mixed experiences with providers during diagnosis, shortages of providers, high costs, and dissatisfaction with school and behavioral supports. Many said caring for their child had hurt their work, and they asked for support groups.
This is one small survey about autism, and it does not cover Minnesota. It points to access and information as barriers, alongside any others.

sources.label: University of Maryland, summary of Adere, Dababnah and Habayeb (2023), Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders

context.heading: A study in the Amhara region of Ethiopia
body: Breffka, Jagoe, Murphy and Tsegaw (2023) combined 16 interviews with a survey of 970 adults with disabilities in community-based programs in three communities in South Gondar, collected from 2018 to 2021. They report restricted participation across many areas of life, and say misconceptions about causes and low expectations of what disabled people can do worsen stigma. The abstract does not say which beliefs were involved. These are adults in programs in Ethiopia and not a picture of Minnesota families.

sources.label: Breffka, Jagoe, Murphy and Tsegaw (2023), African Journal of Disability

context.heading: Holy water priests and a mental health clinic in Addis Ababa
body: Baheretibeb, Wondimagegn and Law (2024) interviewed 12 male holy water priest healers at two Orthodox churches in Addis Ababa in March 2020. The study is about mental illness and not disability in general. The priests gave several explanations at once, spiritual ones along with substance use, physical illness, poverty and trauma. Many said they helped persuade reluctant families to use the clinic, and they credited it with reducing their use of shackles. They also said referrals ran one way. One priest described a patient covered in holy mud being turned away as dirty, and he took that as disrespect.

The authors note the small, all-male, urban sample and that church leaders identified the participants. For staff, the point to carry is a practical one: prayer, holy water and formal services can happen at the same time, so ask without judgment and do not read one as refusing the other.

sources.label: Baheretibeb, Wondimagegn and Law (2024), Transcultural Psychiatry

context.heading: A journalistic account from Ethiopia
body: A 2021 remembrance of the advocate Zemi Yenus in The Transmitter says parents in Ethiopia have reported hearing autism described as a sin, a punishment, a curse or possession, and that mothers are often blamed. It also says autistic children may be kept at home because of stigma. This is a journalist's and colleagues' account and not a research finding. The same piece describes her work with taxi drivers, teachers and parents.

sources.label: The Transmitter, "Remembering Zemi Yenus: An ambassador for autism in Africa" (2021)

context.heading: Enforcement fears in Minnesota in 2026
body: MPR News reported on June 30, 2026, that the Ethiopian Sports Federation's tournament nearly did not come to Minnesota because federal immigration enforcement known as Operation Metro Surge had frightened many community members. This is not a finding about disability services. Say clearly what your program does with personal information, and do not assume what any person fears.

sources.label: MPR News, on the Ethiopian soccer tournament and immigration fears (June 30, 2026)

context.heading: Language and what could not be found
body: The DC-Georgetown University Center for Excellence in Developmental Disabilities produced an Amharic translation of the CDC's Learn the Signs. Act Early. milestone materials in fiscal year 2024. The Multicultural Autism Action Network in Minnesota lists one Amharic-language video, on elopement (wandering) in autistic children. Amharic is written in the Ge'ez script, and some people may read neither Amharic nor English, or may prefer Tigrinya or Afaan Oromo, so ask. Do not use children as interpreters.

No verified source was found for Amharic words for disability, for stigmatizing terms or for preferred terms, so ask the person and use a trained interpreter and not a dictionary. No source was found on who makes decisions in families, so ask each person. Minnesota service directories have listed some providers with an Ethiopian specialization, but none of them could be confirmed.

communityRoutes.name: Multicultural Autism Action Network
communityRoutes.purpose: Family education and support on autism, legislative advocacy, and videos in Amharic, Oromo, Somali and English. Its latest dated event on the page when checked was in 2023, with a 2024 copyright, so call first.

communityRoutes.name: Ethiopian Community in Minnesota
communityRoutes.purpose: Referrals to agencies, help with documents, notary services and first-time renter references. It is not a disability-specific service.

communityRoutes.name: Re'ese Adbarat Tserha Aryam Kidist Selassie Cathedral
communityRoutes.purpose: Lists faith community nursing, mentoring and social services, and parent and family programs. It is a congregation and not a disability service, so ask what is running now. Phone 612-913-7000.

organizations.intro:
Minnesota has no reliable current count of Amharic speakers. The Census Bureau estimated 9,490 Amharic speakers age 5 and older in Minnesota for 2009-2013 (give or take 1,009), seventh among states; since then its standard tables group Amharic with Somali and other Afro-Asiatic languages. Minnesota schools reported 2,379 students with Amharic as their primary home language in 2024-25, 948 of them English learners. MPR reported in 2005 that the State Demographer's office estimated about 7,500 Ethiopian immigrants in the state, and that immigrant groups said the number was about double.

An undated project request to the Minnesota House estimates 45,000 to 50,000 people in and around the Twin Cities who identify as Ethiopian or Ethiopian American, but that is a figure from a funding request, and it counts ethnicity and not language. Not every Ethiopian speaks Amharic as a first language, and Oromo, Tigrinya and Anywaa speakers have their own organizations.

Worthington's daily newspaper reported on an Ethiopian Orthodox congregation there in 2020 and 2022, under the names Menbere Tsehay Saint Mary and Tsadakane Mariam, and neither its current address nor whether these are one congregation could be confirmed.

The list below offers starting points for learning. It is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: Ethiopian Community in Minnesota
entries.purpose: Notary services, help with supporting documents, referrals to agencies, references for first-time renters, civic engagement and Ethiopian cultural activities. Its site lists office hours on Mondays from 9 to 11 a.m. and Fridays from 3 to 5 p.m. A state listing has also given 1821 University Avenue West, Suite 233, so call or write before visiting. A project request to the Minnesota House sought money to buy a community center, and no record was found that a purchase went through.

entries.name: Minnesota Debre Bisrat St. Gabriel and St. Arsema Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
entries.location: Rosemount, 144th Street West; displaced after a fire
entries.purpose: A congregation of about 200 members that moved to Rosemount in April 2026 after outgrowing its St. Paul space. A fire in July 2026 heavily damaged the building, and most of it is expected to be demolished. No one was hurt. FOX 9 reported that members were meeting to pray at a park across the street and that another church had offered space for Sunday services.

entries.name: Ethiopian Evangelical Church in Minnesota
entries.location: Oakdale, 7360 33rd Street North; formerly St. Paul
entries.purpose: Sunday and Wednesday services in Amharic, a Saturday young adult service in Amharic, and a Sunday youth service in English. Its site says it has moved from its earlier location, and it posts sermons on YouTube.

entries.name: Tawfiq Islamic Center
entries.purpose: A center founded by Oromo Muslims from Ethiopia and, by a 2016 Southside Pride report, open to Muslims of any nationality. It is listed here so staff know an Ethiopian Muslim family may have ties beyond the Orthodox and evangelical churches. No Amharic-speaking Ethiopian Muslim association was found.
entries.linkLabel: Ampers segment on Little Oromia, which names the center, 2025

entries.name: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, Minnesota and Surrounding Archdiocese
entries.purpose: The regional body of the church. Kidist Selassie Cathedral says it is under this archdiocese. Worthington's daily newspaper named Abune Ewostatewos as Archbishop of Minnesota and surrounding areas in 2020. No website of its own was found, so ask a parish for the current contact.
entries.linkLabel: Kidist Selassie Cathedral's page, which names the archdiocese

entries.name: Ethiopian Sports Federation in North America
entries.purpose: Runs an annual soccer tournament and cultural festival that began in Houston in 1984. MPR reported more than 20,000 people expected at the 43rd tournament in the Twin Cities area in summer 2026, with 32 teams, and the governor declared July 3 Ethiopian Day.

entries.name: Mahibere Kidusan
entries.location: International, with a North America center
entries.purpose: An association within the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church that supports Sunday schools, monasteries and traditional schools, and produces religious programming in Amharic. Its site was posting in October 2026. Nothing recent was found about Minnesota activity.

entries.name: American Ethiopian Public Affairs Committee
entries.purpose: A political action committee established in March 2021 to promote U.S.-Ethiopia relations, with voter registration, state chapters and a youth group. Its site listed a September 2026 webinar on violence against Christians in Ethiopia. It is one political voice and does not speak for everyone.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: English-language news about Minnesota immigrants and communities of color, including profiles of Ethiopian journalists in the state.

entries.name: KFAI 90.3 FM, Voices of Ethiopia
entries.purpose: The latest KFAI playlist listed for Voices of Ethiopia is from Sunday, April 17, 2022, 4 to 5 p.m., hosted by Ahmed Wassie. The current schedule and the other hosts are unconfirmed.

entries.name: MPR News
entries.purpose: English-language public radio that has covered Ethiopian community events, including the 2026 soccer tournament.

entries.name: ZeHabesha
entries.location: Founded in Minnesota; reaches an international audience
entries.purpose: Ethiopian political and social news, in English articles and Amharic video, founded in 2008 by Henok A. Degfu. Its site was posting in September 2026. It has been sued over interviews it published.

entries.name: EBS TV
entries.location: Started in Silver Spring, Maryland, in 2008
entries.purpose: Amharic entertainment, talk, news and music programming, with live streaming and Roku. Its site showed news items dated October 30, 2026.

entries.name: BBC News Amharic
entries.purpose: News in Amharic on Ethiopia, the Horn of Africa and the world, launched in 2017 alongside Afaan Oromo and Tigrinya services.

entries.name: VOA Amharic
entries.purpose: News for Ethiopia and the diaspora. Its site listed programs dated October 30, 2026. Voice of America has faced federal cuts and court fights, so check it is still running before relying on it.

entries.name: Addis Standard
entries.purpose: Independent news on Ethiopia, under severe pressure. The Committee to Protect Journalists reports that Ethiopia's media authority revoked its registration on February 24, 2026, that its editor-in-chief was detained on August 1, 2026, and that its newsroom was raided on August 2. The publisher is challenging the revocation in court.
entries.linkLabel: Committee to Protect Journalists report, August 2026

entries.name: Tadias Magazine
entries.purpose: English-language news, events, interviews and arts for the Ethiopian American diaspora, founded in 2003. Its site was publishing in August 2026.
